USE OF POSTAL FRANK BY MR. TESSIER-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise in regard to the apparent flagrant misuse of parliamentary members' franking privileges by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue, namely, the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead (Mr. Tessier) in regard to a letter, a copy of which I have here, sent out by Jomac Canada Incorporated of Beebe, Quebec, in which that company has used the parliamentary frank of the member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead for purposes of advocating its opinions on problems facing the Canadian glove industry, such letters as this one being mailed free of charge by use of the frank through the House of Commons post office. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon):
That a complete investigation be made of the abuse of parliamentary free mailing privileges through the House of Commons post office by Jomac Canada Incorporated of Beebe, Quebec, and specifically by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead, Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue, and that such investigation be made by the Speaker and by the Management and Members' Services Committee of the House of Commons with a view to taking whatever action is deemed necessary.

speechtext:

speechtext:

Canadians are today paying their final respects to Terry Fox, an exceptional young man whose courage and determination inspired the nation. At this time many people are proud to honour his memory by pledging donations to the Terry Fox Marathon of Hope. In view of the current postal strike, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis):
That the government do everything possible to make arrangements with the chartered banks and trust companies for the receipt and disbursement of donations made to the Marathon of Hope in memory of Terry Fox.

PETRO-CANADA PRICE OF GASOLINE IN CALGARY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Last Saturday in Calgary the Petro-Canada service station on the McLeod Trail was advertising regular gasoline for 27.8 cents per litre while the Gulf station on Centre Street was selling the same product for 27.4 cents per litre. The government's window on the oil industry has apparently become muddied because of the arrogance of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), because the purchase of Petrofina is costing all car owners four cents extra on every litre of gasoline they buy, etc. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid):
That the government wash its window by cleaning up its act in western Canada prior to taking full operational responsibility for Petrofina in eastern Canada and thus set an example for the industry and give all Canadian consumers the best and lowest possible price.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of some urgency under the provisions of Standing Order 43. It is my understanding that during this postal strike, as in those previous, there is a number of members of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers across the country who have remained on the job, particularly in rural areas. Those who chose this course of action in the past were disciplined, lost their union privileges, and were denied a vote on whether to strike this time. With all due respect to the union, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds-Gren-ville (Mr. Cossitt):
That the Postmaster General use his good office to ensure that those members of CUPW who have chosen to remain on the job will not be discriminated against by senior officials of that union.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATIONS FOR BANK RATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister, and it centres on the bank rate today which has been announced as being relatively static compared with last week, which means that Canada has the
Oral Questions
highest bank rate of any of the seven large industrial nations which will be meeting in Ottawa later this month. Would the Prime Minister indicate how he intends to explain to the other six leaders at the conference why Canada should have the highest interest rate structure in the free western world at a time when many of those leaders have indicated they would like to see a lower interest rate structure rather than the consistently high rate such as that in which Canada has been the leader?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EXPLANATIONS FOR BANK RATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the hon. member is concerned about explanations given to himself, I would point out the Minister of Finance has given them several times. However, he phrases his question in terms of how I would explain this to the other leaders. I can assure him they understand this. They themselves are complaining about the effects on their economies of the very high interest rates in the United States.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATIONS FOR BANK RATE
speechtext: But you are higher.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATIONS FOR BANK RATE
speechtext: They understand, apparently better than the hon. member does, that in Canada, being in such close proximity and so interlinked to the United States, our money markets are much more influenced than others not so closely interlinked. They understand this perfectly well. I think the hon. member should read what is being said and the opinions being voiced in those countries and he will know I will not have to explain that. He should have somebody explain that to him, perhaps a professor of economics in A-l.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATIONS FOR BANK RATE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, obviously the Prime Minister has lost touch with what is happening in North America. His interest rates are substantially above those in the United States. If he wants to follow the American rates, why did he not follow them down?

My supplementary is for the Minister of Finance. As it is generally accepted among economists that the dollar is the key reason why the minister has been maintaining such a high interest rate structure, we note that only last week it was announced that the line of credit the government arranged to sustain the dollar has been increased from $2.5 billion to $3.5 billion. Would the Minister of Finance indicate if that extra billion is in anticipation of continuing pressure on the dollar over the coming months and years, and, if so, would he confirm that will mean not only will we have a dollar under pressure but that the high interest rate structure we now have will likely have to be maintained if some basic changes are not made?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the answer is clearly no, that is not the intention of increasing the stand-by credit. The credit has been in existence for some considerable time. It

July 2, 1981
Oral Questions
was increased in the normal way and does not reflect an expectation that there will be any particular pressure on the Canadian dollar.
The Canadian dollar in recent days and weeks has been above 83 cents. Some people in the country are urging that it be permitted to decline below 83 cents. Because of the state of the Canadian dollar at well above 83 cents, I can assure the hon. member any fears he may have in his mind should be removed.

Madam Speaker, again I direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Bearing in mind we now have a rising personal and corporate bankruptcy rate, and a rising number of foreclosures, would the minister indicate whether he is aware of the fact that he has now allowed real interest rates in this country to be at the highest level since the beginning of the great depression, a real rate of over 5 per cent after inflation is eliminated, compared to the 1979 period when the real rate was 1.2 per cent during the Clark government? If he is aware of that real rate being charged to Canadian consumers, farmers and businessmen, would he indicate when he is going to start showing a little compassion in what he is doing to the average Canadian with his ridiculous policy?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a number of points to make. It would be impossible to deal with all the preamble the hon. member has put into his question because of time limitation, but he talked about rising personal bankruptcies and rising foreclosures. It so happens that last Thursday, I believe it was, I had a meeting with representatives of the mortgage companies in which we explored the mortgage situation, the interest rate situation and the rate of foreclosures. They informed me, based on the statistics they had before them, that the rate of foreclosures on home mortgages this year was lower than last year. So much for rising foreclosures!
How about powers of sale?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: When the hon. member talks about real interest rates and relates his question to the former question about Europe, does he know, for example, that the real interest rate in Germany at the present time is the highest ever experienced by that economy? He ought to put that in his pipe.
I know ours is the highest. Do you agree?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not agree with anything the hon. member puts forward unless I have examined it with binoculars and microscopes, because most of the time it is inaccurate.
The minister knows more about Germany than Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member forgets that a very substantial part of the pressure on interest rates in Canada arises from the strength of the Canadian economy. The great demand for bank loans is still a very substantial pressure on interest rates. If the hon. member wants interest rates to go down a bit, he will ask inflation to come down; that is what will bring it about.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: RENEWAL OF ASSISTED HOME OWNERSHIP PROGRAM MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question. Approximately a year ago the minister said, as reported at page 2176 of Hansard, that the government "would not attempt to solve the economic problems of the country or the fiscal requirements of the government on the backs of the low-income people of this country".
My question concerns the 41,000 Canadians who are by the government's own definition low-income Canadians. They are owners of homes under the Assisted Home Ownership Program. Their mortgages are now up for renewal. The five-year roll-over is due now. Their mortgages were taken out at anywhere from 6 per cent to 8 per cent, and they will be renewed at anywhere from 18 per cent to 19 per cent. In my opinion this represents a tragedy of national dimensions because of the shattered dreams and hopes of people who have to walk away from their homes and write off their investment. The minister has some control over this situation. What action does he propose to take to assist these 41,000 Canadians who must renew mortgages at usurious rates and run the risk of losing their homes and investment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: RENEWAL OF ASSISTED HOME OWNERSHIP PROGRAM MORTGAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in response to the question, the hon. member is about 12 months behind the times. It was at this time last year that the government moved in response to those people who would experience the problems he has indicated. We said to those people who would have to pay a disproportionate amount of their incomes to meet new interest rates, or whatever new charges, those people who would have to pay more than 30 per cent of their income toward shelter costs, that we would continue the subsidies. That program was reintroduced this year for a further 12 months. We have responded to the people who are most in need. We have shown a response to those people. We have used an equitable standard to address that problem.
July 2, 1981

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSIST AHOP HOME OWNERS

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSIST AHOP HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister is the one who is a year behind because there are 500,000 mortgages up for renewal this year. Included in that 500,000 are these 41,000 AHOP mortgages. I doubt there is a member in the House who has not had the experience of an AHOP owner who cannot afford to meet the new mortgage payments.
Because the minister can control the situation, does he intend to take any action whatsoever to change the financing arrangements for these AHOP owners so that they can continue to occupy and to own their homes, rather than walk away from them and hand the keys over to the minister? He knows what is happening, and he can do something about it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ASSIST AHOP HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I indicated that last year the government, in response to the first year of that program, moved to assist those people whose mortgages were rolling over after the end of the first five-year period by using the 30 per cent rule, which I think everyone in the industry accepts as an equitable standard for payment toward shelter needs. After we introduced that, there were relatively few people with the roll-over problem who took advantage of that 30 per cent rule. Further, the number of people in difficulty under that program has reduced this year compared to last year. With respect, Madam Speaker, the hon. gentleman is really 12 months behind the times.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-NECESSITY FOR NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain.

subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-NECESSITY FOR NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-NECESSITY FOR NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, with that kind of an ovation I should be asking the Prime Minister a question. However, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. Given that anyone who understands collective bargaining realizes that a settlement cannot be achieved unless you are at the negotiating table; and given that the open-line radio programs have already started their poison, as they do every time there is a dispute in the public service, undermining the credibility of the entire operation, what is it that the government requires? What conditions has the government set for a return to the negotiating table forthwith?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-NECESSITY FOR NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased the hon. member has raised that question. The negotiating table is there and we are prepared to sit down this afternoon. I wish the hon. member would encourage the postal union to behave the same way. We have been trying to get the postal union to the
Oral Questions
negotiating table since last Friday. We stipulated no conditional precedents to negotiations.
Madam Speaker, can the minister then explain to me what it is that is contained in the Jasmin report which the government does not feel it could implement immediately?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have answered that question in this House concerning the Jasmin report with respect to the government's position on a variety of issues which have been raised in the report. I have also indicated our willingness to discuss certain areas of that report. I would very much appreciate it if the hon. gentleman would encourage his friends in CUPW to return to the negotiating table so that we can explore fully their respective demands and our own.

Madam Speaker, am I then to understand that every matter contained in the Jasmin report would be acceptable to the government under certain conditions? If that is the case can I then assume that all of the matters that were on the bargaining table prior to the breakdown in negotiations are subject to further negotiation, and that the government is prepared to sit down this afternoon in an attempt to find a resolution to this dispute?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have indicated in the past that the government cannot return to the bargaining table under an ultimatum that it will only return if it accepts everything in the Jasmin report. That has been made clear on numerous occasions. It is not the responsibility of members of this House to negotiate a collective agreement here on the floor of this House. I have also made that point, Madam Speaker. However, I would encourage the hon. member to use his good offices and get CUPW back to the negotiating table this afternoon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. Reviewing reports in the press today, the postal workers have regrettably not accepted the call for mediation nor the appointment of a mediator. The proposal is unacceptable to them and the two sides remain deadlocked. There appears, at least on the face of things, that there will not be an early end to this dispute. I ask the minister what plans does the government have to bring this matter to a head so that there can be a return to normal postal service in Canada?

July 2, 1981
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the employees, members of CUPW, are exercising their legal right to strike. I hope this matter will be brought to an end at the negotiation table. That is the natural process. That is the process contemplated by the law. They have the right to strike, and they are exercising it.

subtopic: POSSIBLE INTRODUCTION OF BACK TO WORK LEGISLATION

subsubtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CANADIAN CANCER SOCIETY-POSSIBLE MEANS OF OFFSETTING EFFECTS OF POSTAL STRIKE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The minister will be well aware, as we all are, of the millions of Canadians who have paid and wish to pay further tribute to the memory of Terry Fox. Many of these, as the minister will know, wish to express their very deep feeling by way of contributions to the Canadian Cancer Society. Tragically and unhappily the Canadian postal service situation has deterred many of these Canadians from expressing their feelings in terms of contributions to the society.
I wonder if the minister would consider asking the Canadian chartered banks and other federally incorporated lending institutions to accept donations on behalf of the society, and to permit them to issue temporary receipts until the postal situation permits the Canadian Cancer Society to issue the regular tax receipts.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CONTRIBUTIONS TO CANADIAN CANCER SOCIETY-POSSIBLE MEANS OF OFFSETTING EFFECTS OF POSTAL STRIKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has made a very worth-while suggestion. I will be happy to follow it up to see whether his objective can be realized, or maybe it has already been realized.

speechtext: I thank the hon. minister, because steps have been taken in that direction; but I think it needs a push from the minister to satisfy the requirements of the society.

USE OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING FUNDS TO PROMOTE TERRY FOX CANCER FIGHTING CAMPAIGN
speechtext: My supplementary question is directed to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism, who is responsible for government advertising. He will be aware that several millions of dollars were allocated for a government advertising program for the Constitution, which program now, for obvious reasons, has been postponed. Will the minister consider using a very small portion of these allocated funds to inform Canadians that they may make their contributions to honour Terry Fox to Canadian financial institutions? I hope the minister would agree that he would be hard-pressed to find a more worth-while advertising program for the government and, frankly, hard-pressed to Find one which is more in the interests of national unity.

subtopic: USE OF GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING FUNDS TO PROMOTE TERRY FOX CANCER FIGHTING CAMPAIGN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would be delighted to bring that request to the attention of the Minister of Justice. As the minister responsible for advertising I do not have any direct control over expenditures by particular departments. That is determined by individual ministers in conjunction with ongoing Treasury Board rules. I just have my own budget in multiculturalism, for instance. However, 1 will bring that to the attention of the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF PRICING AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
NEGOTIATION OF PRICING AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Yesterday we had Canada's birthday, and the only present Canadians received was another increase-

subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF PRICING AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
speechtext: Dominion!

subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF PRICING AGREEMENT WITH PROVINCE OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
-another increase in the price of oil by a dollar a barrel. Negotiations which have been going on for some 16 months now, between the Minister and the minister of energy in Alberta appeared to reach a more negative conclusion on Monday than had been the case with the previous meeting. Therefore I say that the minister's well known negotiating talents have again met failure in these negotiations with Alberta.
Since so much is hanging in the balance through not achieving a resolution of this deadlock, can the minister tell the House when he expects there will be some resolution achieved in the negotiations? To put it simply, has he set himself a deadline by which time he must reach an agreement with the province of Alberta?

subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO EXCLUDE RIGHT TO STRIKE PROVISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Postmaster General who will recall that at the time of the committee's consideration of the Provisions of the Canada Post Corporation Act he expressed the great expectation that, with the passage of the act, there would be a greater chance for labour peace in the postal service in Canada. Royal assent was given to the act on April 23 and now, a little over two months later, we have our first strike.
Will the Postmaster General now recognize that some of the representations made to him at committee with respect to the inclusion in that act of provisions that would preclude the right to strike in the postal service have considerable merit and should be considered?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: REPRESENTATIONS TO EXCLUDE RIGHT TO STRIKE PROVISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to correct the words of the hon. member. The act has not yet been proclaimed. It is true that the act was passed by Parliament but it is not yet proclaimed and therefore the corporation has not yet been established. It is too early to see how the union will behave under a Crown corporation because it is not yet under a Crown corporation. It is hoped that will come soon and that labour relations will then be better.
As to the question of whether the union should have the right to strike, I would remind the hon. member, as I did at the time, that there are more illegal strikes in Canada than legal strikes. Just to take away the right to strike of employees does not necessarily avoid strikes. Those who believe very strongly in certain points will not hesitate to use the means at their disposal to register their point, and that could probably be by illegal strikes.

Madam Speaker, I am aware that the act has not been proclaimed. I indicated that it had received Royal Assent on April 23. In any event, what the Postmaster General has indicated is that he has no general faith in a provision in the act itself precluding the right to strike. His colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, has indicated that the government has no intention now of introducing special legislation which would oblige members of the postal service to return to work. How long is the country to wait for the necessary service provided by the Post Office, before the government takes it upon itself to discharge its responsibility to Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: As long as the two parties take to reach a settlement, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: FIRA-BBC BROWN BOVERI CANADA INC.
speechtext:
1.	Is the government aware of a working paper prepared by the Centre for Industrial Relations of the University of Toronto which states that public sector remuneration is six to eight per cent higher than in the private sector?
2.	(a) Have the wages of public sector employees, in recent years, exceeded those of their private sector counterparts by five to fifteen per cent (b) has the wage advantage been larger for females than for males (c) do high-level occupations in the public sector not pay the competitive wage and, if there is an acknowledged differential, does the President of the Treasury Board intend to bring Public Service salaries into line with the private sector?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: FIRA-BBC BROWN BOVERI CANADA INC.
speechtext:
1. The hon. member probably refers to the work of Mr. Morley Gunderson who published a number of papers and articles in professional journals on the subject of public sector compensation.
2. Generally, Mr. Gunderson's studies do not differentiate between employees at the federal, provincial and municipal levels and some of the major conclusions are based on 1971 census data. However, in the discussion of the results, Mr. Gunderson mentions that "the largest wage advantage is at the provincial and local levels, with little or no advantage at the federal level" (Industrial Relations Vol. 19, Number 3, Fall 1980, p. 268) or "Federal wage increases appear to have been the most 'orderly' and 'in line' with private sector wages." He also concludes that the fact the public sector advantage for females is greater than that for males "presumably reflects the lower degree of sex discrimination in the public sector." In addition, he mentions that it "may be a result of a more egalitarian wage policy that is also responsible for the greater wage advantage in low-wage occupations in the public sector" (Industrial Relations, Vol. 19, Number 3, Fall 1980, p. 269).
In concluding that the public sector results do not apply to the federal government, Mr. Gunderson's analysis is consistent with the findings of a recent study by the Conference Board in Canada which, based on more up to date data, indicated that "There is no substantive evidence that suggests rates of pay in the Federal government consistently exceed the rates of pay for comparable jobs in the private sector as of mid-1978" (M. J. Daniel and W. E. A. Robinson, "Compensation in Canada: A Study of the Public and Private Sectors", the Conference Board in Canada, Ottawa, April 1980).
The policy followed by the government as employer in compensating federal employees is comparability with the private sector up to and including the first level of the executive officer category. Above this level, salaries for increased responsibilities are not based on market comparability. They adhere to a system of differentials in recognition of job accountability.

The Liberal party argued it was being overcharged, whereas the Conservative party paid its bills as they were rendered without disputing them. It is obvious there is a charge. speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation we are dealing with today is a small but quite important amendment to the Animal Disease and Protection Act.
To state it simply, this amendment means that owners of livestock will be compensated when animals, which would have been ordered destroyed under the act, die before that order can be carried out. It also provides compensation for the owner of an animal injured while being tested under the act and therefore has to be destroyed. These changes are long overdue.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) raised some interesting arguments about compensation for livestock, but 1 should first point out that the bill we are dealing with does not deal with rates of compensation. It merely closes two loopholes so that farmers, operating under the provisions of the act and complying with its intent, do not lose out when animals die before the process is completed. I am sure the hon. member will agree with the justice in that amendment.
There is a very good reason also for providing a different type of compensation for brucellosis and tuberculosis than for the other diseases named in the act. Brucellosis and tuberculosis are endemic diseases in Canada, and the livestock industry has a certain responsibility to see that its herds are not infected. They are both under eradication programs which, I should point out, have the full support of the livestock producers of this country.
Back in the early 1970s we amended the bill so that farmers would not be locked into statutory compensation rates that require legislation to change. They are now subject to regulation. Those regulations are under constant review by my department and are amended as livestock values change. When animal prices rise to the levels the hon. member suggests, the levels of compensation can be amended. Full market value is paid when the animal is destroyed by an exotic disease because that can in no way be controlled by the producer. By setting a maximum level for animals destroyed under the eradication programs, we place some responsibility on the producer to manage his or her herd in such a way as to keep it
July 2, 1981

free from disease. Animals sold at auctions must show proof of freedom from diseases, so a producer need not introduce diseased animals into the herd.
The program has been successful. Less than 90 herds are now quarantined for brucellosis. That is down from 1,500 herds in 1977. Tuberculosis probably exists in about 10 herds and we expect it will be totally eradicated in the next two or three years.
When producers have high priced animals, Mr. Speaker, we feel they have a responsibility to insure them and such insurance is available. We do not think the taxpayer should have to bear that burden. There is insurance and they should take it, as practically all good breeders do. A good farmer knows that disease is costly. If he allows disease to exist in his herd, he is losing far more money than he will lose by having the diseased animals destroyed and using the compensation to replace them.
We have worked hard to keep our programs up with the times. The hon. member talks about situations as they were in the past. They are very different now, including the pay for veterinarians. Vets in the government service recently negotiated a new two-year contract and I think you will find they have a level of income that relates very well to the income of vets in private practice. That is long overdue and the new contract, in most instances, brings them up to a comparable level. I totally agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain on this. For the education they have, the number of years it takes to be properly trained, many are underpaid because they happen to be a veterinarian working for the Department of Agriculture, whereas someone in another department with less education is paid more because they are working for a department that is considered probably more sophisticated than agriculture. We hope to bring them all in line, whether they be veterinarians, technicians or whatever. There has been a philosophy in the past that says that if you work with food you should take a lesser income. For too long it has been thought that people who work with food are peasants or associates of peasants.
Canada enjoys a very high standard of animal health and this pays dividends not just to the livestock producer but to all Canadians through strong export sales of Canadians animals. Exports of live animals and poultry brought in more than $230 million last year. That is only possible because the Canadian livestock industry has developed a high level of animal hygiene. Our animals are sought out by foreign buyers because they know they are getting healthy, disease-free stock. We claim to have the most disease-free stock in the world and we want to improve on that. It did not come about just by chance, Mr. Speaker. It came about through close co-operation among the federal and provincial agriculture departments, the veterinarians, the livestock producers and the animal and poultry breeding associations all across the country.
In the eradication of disease, it often becomes necessary to destroy livestock. The Animal Disease and Protection Act gives us the authority to do that. But if you are to destroy a farmer's livestock, you have to compensate him for the loss.
Animal Diseases
The levels of compensation paid for animals ordered destroyed in disease-control programs has been increased from time to time to reflect rising livestock prices, the latest being last December when maximums for purebred dairy and beef cattle were raised to $1,800 and $1,500 respectively. Last year my department paid out a little more than $5 million in compensation to livestock producers.
When we talk about the importance of livestock producers to the over-all economy, we would do well to remind ourselves just how important it is. Farm cash income from cattle and calves last year was $3.8 billion or about 25 per cent of total farm cash income. Income from hog production was $1.4 billion, or 9 per cent of farm cash receipts. Add in poultry and dairy products and it comes to $8.3 billion or 54 per cent of farm income. In our society we hear so often that grain is the largest source of farm income. Mr. Speaker, it is not. The livestock and poultry industry are, as I said, 54 per cent of total farm income. Then you have the horticultural crops, the fruits and vegetables, which are quite large and ever expanding. So we see a change in livestock production but 1 do not think we should ever underestimate the value of that industry to our society.
We also know how much it means to the feed industry. Canadian feed manufacturers' figures show they sell approximately $1.8 billion worth of feed to the livestock producers in Canada. They are huge users of feed grains in Canada.
As I said before, the bill before the House today, Mr. Speaker, brings into the act two situations under which owners may lose out on compensation payments even though coverage of these losses falls within the intent of the act. As the act is now written, if an animal is inspected by a veterinarian and found infected, but dies before it can be destroyed, then the owner is not eligible for compensation. Similarly, an owner loses out if his animal is injured while being tested for an infectious or contagious disease and must be destroyed. This may sound strange to some people but some animals not in close contact with humans are under tremendous stress when they are put in pens, etc., and some become frightened and die. Under the old act there was no way properly to compensate the farmers for that. We think that is unfair. It rarely happens but it is a tremendous loss when it does. Surely those owners are entitled to the compensation they would have received if their animals had completed the testing process and been destroyed under the act.
The amendments the House is being asked to approve today, Mr. Speaker, will legalize the payments of compensation to those qwners. It is not a big item in terms of the money require^. The compensation for animals destroyed under these situations represents less than 2 per cent of the value of compensation currently being paid. Some people say I have been right and I have been wrong: I have been right in making these payments but I was wrong because I did not have the propej^gislation to do it. I have said one can never get into difficulty when they are right in making a payment, no matter what it complies with.

July 2, 1981
Animal Diseases
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members will be quick to approve these short, but important changes in an act that has been such a benefit to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess I do not now have any farmers in my constituency, although I have had in years gone by, so it is very difficult to speak on behalf of the people I represent. However, I do want to say a word or two about the bill.
My understanding of it is now quite clear, having listened to the minister. I appreciate the fact that he spoke ahead of me because I did not want to misinterpret him. At one stage, while reading the bill I frankly misinterpreted one of the sections. As I understand it, this bill is more or less a response to a series of situations which have arisen over the last few years as to whether or not compensation could or could not be paid under the act. The act as it existed did not take into account very grey, fringe areas where animals died prior to action being taken by Department of Agriculture officials to determine the health of the animal. 1 was particularly interested in the speech of the hon. member the night before last. He talked about the problems of price maintenance in a number of different areas.
Recently I had occasion to tour the farming community in my area. A discussion took place concerning a young man who had undertaken some two years ago to establish a hog farming operation. I raise this matter only as an aside; it is related indirectly. The young man went to the bank and borrowed funds in order to get his hog farm under way. He had a fairly substantial and well-run operation. He is a dedicated young farmer whose background is in farming. Now he is in considerable debt. If he were less dedicated, I wonder what care and maintenance his animals would receive. The rate of return on his farming endeavour is not sufficient at this point to cover his outlay. This situation could quite easily lead a less dedicated individual to care in a much more cursory manner for the health of his animals.
Also my colleague in the Conservative party referred to a matter which closely ties in with the health of animals. If farmers are unable to receive a reasonable return for the sale of animals-in this case pigs and hogs-they must become more part time and less full time farmers; they spend more and more of their time working at other things. I am referring to a fairly small operation. Then the level of care and the investment of time are dramatically reduced. If I read the situation correctly, the end result could lead to animal diseases not being detected early. Therefore this could add to the problem of the need to dispose of more diseased animals than would otherwise be necessary. I realize this is somewhat a branch-off in terms of the present discussion, but we must look at this as part of a total package.
If farmers, particularly animal farmers, are to be primarily responsible for early identification of diseased animals, we cannot continue to allow an erosion of the price structure to the point at which farmers cannot devote full time to their
farms. This is in support of much of what the minister has said concerning price maintenance. Farmers should be able to receive a return for their time, effort, financial commitment, investment and bank borrowing charges. These items are rolled into one large investment. Farmers should receive an amount which is sufficient to pay back their loans, to recover their operating costs and to maintain a level of income. If not, they are forced to become part time farmers. Then they will not be present on the premises all the time to care for their animals, particularly the ones which are penned as opposed to those which are roaming, grazing, etc. The minister indicated the millions of dollars he has paid out in the last year. If we consider the last number of years, it may well rise in relationship to the decrease in the amount of care farmers are able to give. I see the minister shaking his head, but let me tell him that I visited two or three farms. I had represented the area for the better part of 13 years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION PAYMENTS
speechtext: Provincially?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING COMPENSATION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Yes, provincially. In my tour I noticed with interest that as farmers are less able to recover sufficiently from their involvement and as they are forced to do other than farm for a living, the level of care of animals definitely decreases. There is no doubt in my mind that this is happening. The minister should take a quick tour of some of the smaller operations. I am not talking about large farms with hired help; I am talking about the smallers ones in which this problem arises primarily. There is a definite decrease in the level of care of animals in that farmers are not present and working full time at their operations.
As we look at the legislation before us, we must take into account the problems which have arisen over the last while. I suggest that between now and five years from now, if we allow the price structure to continue below a fair rate of return, more and more farmers will be put in the position of not being able to maintain their operations at the level to which they are committed. Therefore more and more animals will receive less care than they otherwise would have received. The end result of this situation could well be a requirement on the part of the government through this legislation to expend considerably larger sums of money than are currently being expended in order to deal with the problem of diseased animals.
I am trying to extrapolate what I have seen in a very small area into a much larger concern. I would not rule it out because it is not an exact comparison. If one looked at the effect of abandoned orchards on the orchards which are still operating, one would quickly recognize that the problem of diseased trees had a very serious effect upon neighbouring orchards. The farmers in the Niagara Peninsula-and I suspect those in Essex County-found it virtually impossible to continue their orchard operations given the prices they received for the product they produced. The end result was that they backed away from their fruit farms. They did not walk away one day; they gradually harvested less and less. As they gradually produced less and less, they received fewer and fewer dollars and put less into pesticides and other treatments
July 2, 1981

necessary to maintain the health of the trees. Little by little the erosion took place. 1 am not a farmer, but I have some experience in that area. I am concerned that if smaller farmers are not able to recover sufficient income from their products, they will similarly be unable to maintain their business operations. They will not be able to put the time, the effort or, for that matter, the concern into farming. Although we will not have to amend this act any more because the payment is no longer statutory, I suspect that over the course of time we will find considerably larger and larger sums of money allocated for the eradication of disease which was brought on simply by an inadequate price structure in the first place.
I support the minister in some of what he has said in the past, but we have to find a way to do one of two things, or perhaps a combination of two things. We have to find a way to make it possible for the smaller family farm wanting to maintain its operation and take its produce to market to do so. First, we have to find a way to guarantee that there will be a reasonable price paid to farmers for the time and the effort they spend on their operation. Second, we have to find a way to reduce the numbers of dollars farmers must hand out to banks and the like, if I may say, for the money they must ultimately borrow to maintain their operations in a way that will be satisfactory both to them and to the marketplace.
I readily admit that the bill deals quite specifically with one change in a series of different sections. I can see that unless we go much further, unless we do something about the economics of farming, not only will we be dealing with diseased livestock eradication problems, but I suspect we will be dealing, at least in some parts of this country, with diseased grain and other problems since farmers will not be able to put the time, the money or the effort into the protection necessary to safeguard their very livelihood. Knowing the minister's interest in this, I thought I might tie the two together so that he can get back to his colleagues and argue for a better system.
If I may return to the young man I spoke about earlier, here was a young fellow who went to the bank on his own. He went through agricultural college and graduated. He then decided that he would go into hog farming in a reasonable way. He got himself a barn, cleaned it up and put in new pens. He borrowed $20,000. That may not seem like a lot of money to the minister, I do not know, but it seems a lot to me. The young man began carefully, single-handedly, nurturing and building his herd. The problem is the young man has no place for his herd now because he cannot get his money back in the marketplace. I must stress that it is his personal dedication only that keeps him on the land and keeps him trying to make his undertaking a viable one.
1 think it would be useful if the House of Commons would spend a little more time, as I have said on a number of other issues, in dealing with that problem. The problem does not confront the larger farms. In many instances large farms are able to self-finance because of their size. But it certainly confronts the young, eager farmers who are trying to make a
International Development Association go of it and maintain our food supplies. Maybe we could find a way to accommodate their concerns. In the long run money would be saved under this legislation in the marketplace.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF DEMAND NOTES
speechtext:
that Bill C-71, to amend the International Development Association Act, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to the Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to present to the House a proposed amendment to the International Development Association Act to authorize a payment of $164,600,000 to the International Development Association. As hon. members know, the acronym IDA is commonly used to refer to that association. The payment of that amount will be made as a partial settlement of Canada's commitment in respect of the sixth replenishment of the resources of the association. Support for the International Development Association is one of the main channels through which Canada promotes the development of Third World countries.
As an agency of the World Bank responsible for granting preferential loans, the association has made a name for itself as being one of the most efficient international development multilateral instruments. Indeed, since its creation in 1960, this organization has put up over $20 billion in American funds to carry out various projects, be they related to technical studies or medical research. Seeing how successful the association has been in marshalling resources from the four corners of the world, and especially in profitably investing those resources in the world's least advanced countries, Canada ranked it high in its over-all development assistance program.
All the other major donor countries followed in Canada's footsteps and it is imperative that Canada and the other countries continue to support the International Development Association if we want to maintain the economic growth of underprivileged nations. Although 121 countries belong to the association, the main beneficiaries of the loans made by the

July 2, 1981
International Development Association association are the least developed and very poor countries, namely the few countries where the per capita income is below $625 in 1978 American dollars. The International Development Association is in a position to contribute effectively to the growth of those countries for two reasons. First, it does benefit from the wide experience of the World Bank staff. Second, thanks to its considerable resources, it can develop and implement projects of a scope that no other preferential loan organization could match. The resources of the International Development Association come mostly from the member countries of the OECD, which have provided approximately 95 per cent of its total funds for many years. The loans granted by the World Bank to support these funds for the implementation of projects are usually interest free. Repayment is over 50 years and can start only 10 years after the loan is granted.
Since the Bank exhausts the resources of the IDA by granting such loans, it must regularly replenish the funds of the International Development Association. The total amount needed to replenish these funds as well as the proportional contribution of each country are determined by international negotiations. Afterwards, the respective governments of the member countries are asked to approve the amounts negotiated. This is the sixth current replenishment of the resources since the creation of the International Development Association. In the last few years, the funds of the IDA have been replenished every three years; the sixth replenishment was negotiated in 1979, it will occur in phases from the middle of 1980 until the middle of 1983 and the total amount for that replenishment has been set at $12 billion in U.S. funds.
During the negotiations, Canada decided to set its share at 4.3 per cent of the total replenishment or $601.8 million Canadian. For all previous reconstitutions, Canada's share was just over $1 billion U.S., or 5.3 per cent of the total resources of the International Development Association. The amendment to the International Development Association Act now being considered in this House aims at authorizing the second payment to be made as a partial settlement of Canada's commitment in respect of the sixth replenishment of the resources I have been referring to. Last year, Canada made a first payment of $177.1 million to the Association.
I would like to note, Mr. Speaker, that these payments are made in the form of non-interest bearing demand notes which the International Development Association usually cashes over a period of 10 years as it actually implements its projects. The International Development Association does not need the contribution of Canada immediately, but it asks that we make the unconditional commitment to pay these funds by issuing noninterest bearing demand notes to be able to make loan agreements with the receiving countries.
The payment by Canada would normally become due on July 1. However, the United States has been late in ratifying the sixth replenishment. To enable the IDA to continue its loan program, Canada and many other donor countries have
made their first payment in respect of the sixth replenishment last year, as provided by the negotiated resolution and as I have just indicated. This year, donor countries have decided to wait for the United States to duly approve their share of the sixth replenishment before making their second payment. The American administration expects Congress to approve its contribution this fall, at which time other donor countries should make their second payment. Until such time as the United States has obtained legislative approval of its commitment to the Association, Canada will be under no obligation to make its second payment, for which authority is now being asked, to the House of Commons. I wish to thank hon. members and the House leaders of the opposition parties for having agreed to limit their speaking time in order to pass this bill, and I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your patience in listening to me.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF DEMAND NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity to reply briefly on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition with respect to this bill. Before I begin my short remarks on the subject, I would like to say that it would be beneficial for us to read at some point the report on the House of Commons by the Auditor General for the fiscal period ending March 31, 1979. In it he wrote rather emphatically and eloquently about the necessity for Parliament having some control over the expenditures of government. We should remind ourselves that the reason we are involved in this series of bills under the arrangements which have been made is not that there is any disagreement in the House of Commons with the kinds of programs which are covered in these bills, as extensive and wide-ranging as they are, but that there was another great disagreement in the House.
It is a credit to the everlasting good name of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) that the government has been brought to the point where it can no longer use dollar items in the estimates. I know the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) will remember what I am saying. The government can no longer use dollar items in the estimates, or authorize expenditure of money, virtually without parliamentary approval. We are engaged in this practice, with respect to this bill to amend the International Development Association Act, because of the necessity to generally observe the requirements of the Auditor General. We want to ensure that Parliament has some control and that the process is right-not just that the ends are justified, but that the means to get to those ends are justified. It is in that spirit that I am very pleased to clearly indicate our support for the bill itself.
Your Honour and I had an opportunity during a parliamentary recess to speak with the minister of education for Somalia at a luncheon. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bock-stael) was there as well. The minister told us of the great difficulties which some countries were facing, and particularly his country, with the influx of people across their borders in a horde, which is hard for us to imagine. I gathered these
July 2, 1981

refugees were from Ethiopia. The economy of his country was supporting, according to the figures and the proportions, the equivalent of an influx into Canada of about eight million people within one year.
I have never forgotten that statistic nor that luncheon. That had a profound effect upon me with respect to the importance of Canada's place in the world and Canada's responsibility as a world nation and as a part of the brotherhood of man. That luncheon and those statistics have been emblazoned on my mind. We were looking into the face of a minister of a small country who was telling us of the enormity of the problem. Could we imagine what would happen in Canada if we had that, burden to bear, just financially, with an economy as strong as ours in comparative terms? It is no wonder that Somalia and other countries are the beneficiaries of what I think is a first-rate offshoot of the World Bank, which is a gathering of nations of the world to help each other.
The International Development Association is a new affiliate of the bank. It was established to meet the situation of a growing number of less-developed nations, those countries in which need for and ability to make use of outside capital is greater than their ability to service conventional loans.
Consequently, the terms of the IDA's development methods are designed so that they will impose less burden on the balance of payments of borrowing countries and of conventional lenders. If we do not have this kind of thing, then loans would be meaningless to some of the countries to which they are addressed.
The association has been described somewhere as a "soft-loan window" used by the World Bank group to lend funds to the poorest developing countries for development purposes at highly concessional rates-a three-quarters of 1 per cent carrying charge, with a 50-year term and [DOT] ten years of grace, is quite an advantage. It is an advantage which I am sure is absorbed and offset by the state of the donor countries. By June 30, 1980, Canada had advanced a total of U.S. $1,027,351,000 to IDA. That represents 5.27 per cent of total donor advances. This bill will allow that to continue.
When preparing for this short debate, Mr. Speaker, I did some reading about something which arose out of a process which is relatively new. I am proud to say that it was initiated in Parliament when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was Prime Minister. I refer to the select committees which the government has now chosen to call parliamentary task forces.
In the third report of the parliamentary task force on North-South relations, stress was laid on the need for a fresh approach to development. It is interesting that the parliamentarians involved, members of the Liberal Party of Canada, members of the Progressive Conservative Party and members of the New Democratic Party, attacked the conundrums facing the nations of the world in an intellectual way as they involve the North-South dialogue.
International Development Association
In that third report, the mixture of members of this House made some recommendations which were unanimous and which other members of this House ought to consider very carefully. They asked for a new approach to development. They asked the House and the country to consider that the image of a world divided between a powerful north and weak and dependent south is outdated and that the country reconsider its position. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has come to this rather late in his public life but it is to be noted that Parliament supported those recommendations.
Some of the key recommendations ought to be remembered and the report ought not to lie fallow in the desks, in the filing drawers and on the shelves of some department of government. The problem with the select committee provisions, when this party was the government, and with the parliamentary task force provisions now, is that there is no way that members of the committee and Parliament can ask the government to respond to the reports adopted by the House within a short period of time. That failure cannot be laid to the Minister of State for Finance; it is the fault of the system.
When we consider parliamentary reform, then, as well as giving Parliament a greater right to hold government financially accountable, I think we ought to give Parliament an opportunity to hold government accountable in the sense that it should respond to and comment upon, in a public way, reports presented to the House. This applies particularly to special reports commissioned as the result of a reference from the government.
The first key recommendation was that Canada should raise its ODA target to .7 per cent of GNP by 1990 and achieve the level of .57 per cent by 1985. It now stands at .46 per cent. If the report were approved and adopted it would increase the current aid budget of $1.2 billion to about $3 billion by 1985. That is a tremendous adjustment but it is an indication of the magnitude of the problem that a committee of Parliament found. It would mean the expenditure of $350 million more than the government envisages at the present time.
The report made a second and very important recommendation, that Canada should concentrate its aid on the poorest countries, giving its highest priority to basic education and improving women's skills. This is something which is needed in every country but particularly in the poorest countries. It is the message that the minister of education of Somalia left with us, aside from the basic needs message that he brought. We now support 89 countries. The thrust of the report is that we should concentrate on fewer countries.
There is also a recommendation that more of the ODA should go to non-governmental organization activities, notably to smaller rural projects operated by NGOs on CIDA's behalf.
It recommended that CIDA should decide where to buy goods and services favouring Canadian sources, but free of any percentage rule such as is in place at the moment. It proposed that short-term commercial objectives should not be permitted to undermine the developmental objectives of aid. There is a

July 2, 1981
International Development Association
sense of humanity running through all that, the thrust of it being that there would be a long-term benefit to Canada.
Food aid should only be used to fill the gap between a country's food needs and its food production. Canada should buy food for needy nations from neighbouring poor countries having surplus food.
The report went on to say that there should be a major public inquiry to pin-point industries unable to withstand competition from cheap imports from the Third World. Canada's declining industries ought to be replaced by new, promising enterprises, thereby strengthening Canada's economy and allowing easier entry of developing nations' products. Whether we like it or not, Mr. Speaker, that is something that we are going to have to consider. When I hear members of the government say that we are going to consider an industrial strategy, I wonder what the thrust of it is going to be and how the government will come to terms with that very significant recommendation, which is a difficult one for this country at this time.
The report gave some credence to the importance of the price of energy and the supply of energy. It recommended that we should support the creation of a new energy-related lending agency as proposed by the World Bank. I think that is important in view of the cost of energy and its effect on the economies of developing countries.
The unanimous report pointed out that we are on the threshold of a new world. Since the report was unanimous, I think it cannot be ignored when considering our external affairs policies, external aid policies, the direction of CIDA, our energy policy. If it means anything at all, then the report must be taken into account by government.
When considering an industrial "policy" and an industrial "strategy"-which I think are two of the most overworked words in Canadian public life-I think it is important to know that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) is examining that recommendation. If it were adopted, the impact on Canadian manufacturing and industry would be imperative, difficult and swift. I do not know to what extent that will happen, but since Parliament has spoken on the matter, it is important that someone respond. We should know what the position of the government is in the short term and in the long term.
The bill is worthy of support, Mr. Speaker. Except for the process, it was worthy of support even when it was a dollar item, but the process got in its way. As a result, we have agreed with respect to this series of legislation to put these bills through quickly. This is one of them. The impact that the plight of some underdeveloped countries can have on anyone, even the most hardshelled, is difficult to express. This bill and the program is designed to permit Canada to do its reasonable share as a citizen of the world.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ISSUANCE OF DEMAND NOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for his explanation. He certainly made it very clear. I say to the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton
(Mr. Baker) that it was a very interesting series of observations which he made and certainly well worth supporting.
In thinking back over the last few years, we have come a long way in Canada in raising the level of public awareness of the value of aid. Thinking back 15 years, I remember the numerous times that I received communications from irate citizens who wanted to know why we were taxing them so heavily and then handing out the money. Over the course of the last few years we have been able to more easily get the message through to people about the tremendous amount of value that we receive from the few dollars we actually ever send outside of the country.
A number of things have happened. Even yet there is still a level of misunderstanding with which we must deal. We really ought to spend more time with the public making them aware of the kinds of conditions that exist in those countries of the world which qualify for aid under this program and a number of others.
I do not think people are aware of the economic conditions and personal hardships faced by so many of their fellow mortals in other parts of the world. The more recent opportunities for travel have tended to broaden the knowledge of Canadians and to soften the hardened attitudes that were evident some years ago. Nevertheless, we still have a lot to do.
In spite of the fact that our economic conditions are not all they might be, I do not think the people of Canada fully understand the very serious economic deprivation which exists in many other parts of the world. When we think of economic hardship, we tend to talk about it in the context of the Canadian experience. We tend to think of economic hardship along the lines of the hardship we might come into contact with on a day-to-day basis. It is only when you go outside the country and travel in other parts of the world that you begin to fully understand the personal problems that exist and what little we do-and it is little compared to what we could do-to try and assist in ameliorating these conditions in other parts of the world. It is money well spent.
If there was a way for the House of Commons to actually pass judgment on the individual expenditures that are put before us, I do not doubt for a moment that there would be a move by a lot of Canadians, and I think the majority, to increase Canada's involvement in areas such as are affected by the IDA fund.
There are some things we have to try to understand. We have to try to get Canadians to appreciate that in giving assistance, we must not attempt to infringe on the distinctiveness of the people's culture, the way in which they develop. We must not attempt to make them like us. It is not a process of trying to make everyone the same, but of trying to assist in the most basic, human way, trying to provide the wherewithal for self-sufficiency in the most basic areas. It is trying to assist in the level of skilled development, trying to improve, as my colleague said, the educational process for people in many other parts of the world so that they can develop a self-sufficiency.
July 2, 1981

It is not a matter of turning them into Canadians in a different part of the world. It is matter of allowing them to be what they are, assisting them to develop that process so that they will be self-sufficient. Surely it is an attempt to assist them in reducing the amount of health hazard and the problems which continue to exist in their countries, possibly because of bad water supplies or inadequate or immediate access to emergency health care.
I hope Canadians will support this attempt when they see it in the proper context to ensure that those things that we take and have taken for granted for years are available to people in other parts of the world.
We have to guard against the tendency of allowing the assistance we give to be used for exploitation. That tendency is there. No matter how carefully we might speak against allowing that to happen, I have seen evidence of it. I am sure other members of this House of Commons have seen evidence of it as they travelled throughout the world.
Recently I made a visit to an area that might qualify under this aid program. Actually it is not an aid program but could be an aid program. It is subject to repayment. It may take a while, but it is subject to repayment over the long haul.
I was in St. Lucia about eight months ago where I had occasion to meet with the minister there. He took us around the island to show us some of the devastation that had occurred as the result of a hurricane. Living in Canada where hurricanes are an infrequent occurrence, it is hard to imagine how an area can be devastated and how much can be done with a small amount of money.
I recall seeing homes that by Canadian standards were certainly not the most substantial, not the type seen here. Nevertheless they were the homes of the people. These homes had been blown off the face of the earth by this hurricane. I saw banana plantations where considerable sums of money had been spent over the last few years so that the export of bananas could be developed as their main source of income. One fell swoop and away went their income source for at least a year, and probably for two or three years to come.
As I spoke with the prime minister there and the members of his government, I thought of how much we could have done to help relieve the terrible burden those people will have to carry. Instead of devoting quite as much money to advertising in order to praise ourselves for our great efforts, it would be nice if some was spent in bringing to the attention of Canadians those conditions we are attempting to help resolve with what, on balance, are very small sums of money being contributed by each and every Canadian.
I think if we could do that we would find that Canadians would, rather than asking that we reconsider because they are afraid we are spending too much, ask us to reconsider because we are spending too little. I think if they had the facts firmly before them that might be the case.

I want to add a cautionary note. If for no other reason than that it is in our own self-interest to attempt to raise the economic levels of those people, because that will have a spin-off beneficial effect to Canada in years to come if they become "have" rather than "have-not" parts of the world and their consumer purchasing power is increased-if that were the only reason why we were doing it, and I would hope, God, that that is not the only reason, but even for the most mercenary reasons when individuals are looking at the expenditure of some hundreds of millions of dollars over the next period of time, it would be worthwhile.
I want to say to the minister that we are, of course, happy to support this bill. We think that come next year, with no constitutional debate, no oil policy problems, no interest rate problems-I assume all of these things will be behind us-

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) ASSISTANCE ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-74, to authorize financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a bill entitled "An act to authorize financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions", authorizing various payments to international development institutions often known as international financial institutions or, in some cases, regional development banks. The ruling brought down by Madam Speaker on June 12 following a point of order concerning the procedural acceptability of certain items contained in the Main Estimates for 1981-82 obliges us to table this bill. Madam Speaker did indeed rule Items L45 and L60 for External Affairs contrary to our rules and regulations. [English]
Section 2 of the act would provide authority to make two types of payments out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. First, payments in cash of an amount not exceeding $4 million. In fact, the intention is to make only one such payment in fiscal year 1981-82 to the United Nations Common Fund for Commodities. This tranche of $4 million would be the first of three equal payments for the period 1981-82 to 1983-84. The purpose is to support the common fund's second window which will finance measures other than stocking in the field of commodities. The vast majority of benefits from the operations of the fund's second window will flow to the developing countries.
The second type of payment to be authorized under this act involves the issuance, in accordance with terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, of non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes to international financial institutions. The form of these demand notes would be determined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in line with the Financial Administration Act. It is a long-standing practice to make payments to the regional development banks by way of demand notes since they do not require all of the cash at the time of payment. Rather, the cash is needed over a period of up to ten years as the banks make project commitments and actual expenditures are incurred in developing countries. It is with this in mind that encashment schedules for these notes are drawn up and agreed between the international financial institutions and Canada.
As the House will note, clause 2 of this legislation envisages in fiscal year 1981-82 the issuance of non-negotiable demand notes not exceeding in the aggregate $121.2 million. This consists of the following components: first, an amount of $3.5
million for the Caribbean Development Bank's special development fund. This is the last of three tranches to fulfil a Canadian commitment of $10.5 million for the period 1979-80 to 1981-82. Second, a payment of $30 million to the African Development Fund. This is the third and last instalment totalling $85 million over the period 1979-80 to 1981-82. Third, a payment of $56.7 million to the Asian Development Fund. This is the third of four instalments which total $193.4 million for 1979-80 to 1982-83. Fourth, a payment of $17 million to the fund for special operations of the Inter-American Development Bank. This is the third of four payments toward a commitment of $58.1 million in U.S. funds over the years 1979-80 to 1982-83. Fifth, an amount of $14 million for the International Fund for Agricultural Development as the first of three instalments totalling $42 million.
The third clause of this bill deals with the matter of the previously issued non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes referred to earlier. The issuance of these notes in previous years would be ratified and confirmed by this bill. The encashment schedules for the various international financial institutions indicate that an amount of some $19.3 million would be drawn down in the course of fiscal year 1981-82. [Translation]
Clause 4 of the bill would authorize Canada to make an initial subscription for shares of the African Development Bank. Though we have been financing, for some years already, the African Development Fund, its preferential aid mechanism, the Bank decided recently that the considerable development needs of the continent would require a far greater contribution in resources. Accordingly, the African Development Bank will accept in its ranks not only the countries of the area but also countries such as Canada and other donors of the OECD. In view of our active role with both anglophone and francophone countries in Africa, I shall be particularly happy to see Canada sit as a member of the African Development Bank.

Our share in the African Development Bank will be 3.2 per cent of the expanded capital stock. This legislation provides for the purchase of 4,200 paid-in shares over five years as well as 12,600 callable shares. These shares are valued in aggregate at 168 million units of account, for approximately $240 million Canadian. Of this amount only 25 per cent will be paid in; that is approximately $60 million over five years. We will be utilizing the usual method for payments to the African Development Bank.
The fifth and last clause of this legislation conveys authority to issue to the bank this year non-negotiable demand notes equivalent in aggregate to 8.4 million units of account, which equals approximately $12 million Canadian.
In conclusion, for the information of hon. members I would like to add that in fiscal year 1981-82 the sum of $31.3 million will be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund for the encashment of notes previously issued. Authority exists under
