section 45 of the Financial Administration Act for these payments.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) ASSISTANCE ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-74, to authorize financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions, but in doing so I wish to point out one of the incongruities which exists as far as this bill is concerned and as far as the previous bill, Bill C-71, which we were debating, is concerned. That bill, which was to amend the International Development Association Act, and this one, which authorizes financial assistance to certain international financial institutions, both deal with the funding available from Canadian public funds to international financial institutions.
This certainly was an issue I tried to tackle during the time I held the office of Secretary of State for External Affairs, and it is one which I hope the present minister is trying to regularize in trying to bring these two advances through international financial institutions under the aegis of the Department of External Affairs where they both belong. Then the amount of foreign aid and foreign developmental assistance-it goes beyond aid to include developmental assistance as well-will be channelled through one agency or department and not fractionalized between two departments, so that a true and concise picture of our over-all program is given in what we are doing in the field of financial assistance through international institutions to countries of the Third World.
I see the minister is nodding. I hope he is carrying on that effort to try to bring the International Development Association Act, IDAA, under the jurisdiction of his department. In fact, when we get into Committee of the Whole on this bill, I would like to put that question to the minister, and I will welcome any comment he has to make about it. I am reminded by my House leader that the minister also has the opportunity to comment on this when he closes the debate.
This bill has been placed before us, not primarily because of the initiative the government has taken in this regard, but because it came about through my party's prompting through the efforts of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and the ruling of the Chair on June 12. If neither of those two actions had been taken, these items in Bill C-74 might have slipped by the House under the guise of votes L45 and L60 of the Department of External Affairs.
The thought that that might very well have happened if Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition had not been on its toes has very serious implications for the parliamentary system, for it touches on what Michael Valpy of The Globe and Mail last week called, and I quote: "the heart of parliamentary democracy, the central issue of how much scrutiny Parliament should have over what government does".
It is not by chance that there are procedural differences between approving estimates on the one hand and enacting legislation on the other. The first action funds the status quo, while the second action changes it. The difference is a very fundamental one. To confuse the difference by bypassing one
International Financial Assistance
process through using another, quicker method surely only serves to undermine parliamentary responsibility.
This is what we are returning to by debating these bills today. We are giving authority to enact changes in legislation, which is Parliament's responsibility, and I am glad to see this being carried out. To bring in what should be statutory change by the process set up for fund appropriation allows government to step into programs and enter new areas without the proper debate such government initiatives warrant.
Two such initiatives were votes L-45 and L-60 of the external affairs estimates. These are now transferred to Bill C-74. In Madam Speaker's words found on page 10546 of Hansard, what those votes sought to achieve was:
-to finance international development by the use of issuing demand notes to the credit of the various named banks or institutions upon which they may draw in the Bank of Canada, or to purchase shares in the listed banks.
Those votes did not seek merely the simple appropriation of funds, but sought the legislative authority to incur Crown debts without parliamentary approval. The process we are now involved in corrects that major oversight.
Having said this, I want to indicate my party's support for the measure before us. Bill C-74 initially represents $137 million in Canadian investments and advances to financial institutions for international development. It means that the Caribbean Development Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and the International Fund for Agricultural Development can now draw on Canadian government funds for additional contributions totalling some $121 million.
All these contributions are in the nature of advances and are thus repayable after a specified period of time. All items involve non-interest bearing, non-negotiable demand notes to be encashed at a later date. It is appropriate that Canadian contributions should be made through the regional development banks of the areas concerned. I want to re-emphasize that point, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian contributions should be made through the regional development banks of the areas concerned. The regional development bank is an institution which has been developing in the last number of years and has been carrying out a tremendous amount of good work, empowered as it is by funds from the wealthier countries of the world. That, sir, is as it should be.
However, in addition to the $121 million to be put into these regional development banks, some $12 million will go to buying shares in the African Development Bank. This is quite a new procedure. The African Development Bank, like the other regional development banks, is a significant force in the development activities of Africa. It was set up in 1964 by the United Nations Commission for Africa. Since it first began its operations in 1966 it has had significant success, and those who have followed its development will see what it has meant to countries throughout Africa, particularly the poorest parts. With an authorized capital of $1,052 million U.S., subscribed capital of $930 million, and paid-up capital of $295 million, it

July 2, 1981
International Financial Assistance
has been able to assist needy African countries with readily obtainable loans for development projects.
Until 1978 capital stock in that bank could only be held by African countries. This policy is being changed and the $12 million requested in Bill C-74 is in anticipation of that change being completed this year. Non-African countries will then be able to buy into the capital stock of the bank. This is the reason why one cannot find this expenditure in last year's estimates and why this item has been considered by the Speaker as governmental action and not simple fund appropriation. The government is authorizing the investment of money where it has never invested before. It is moving into an area where it has never taken action before.
If this item had gone through under the estimates then it would have set a precedent, in that all future investments in the African Development Bank would be votable items. Parliamentary authority would clearly have been circumvented in that case.
Bill C-74 represents $137 million in advances and investments by the Canadian government towards international development. That, sir, is 89 per cent of total CIDA contributions to international financial institutions for 1981-82. That is not 89 per cent of total CIDA contributions, but 89 per cent of the contributions which CIDA makes through international financial institutions.
Now, Sir, this is the kind of massive commitment that deserves the attention of the House, not necessarily to find fault with it because this specific financial disbursement indeed has merit. Rather, the House needs to consider this kind of massive investment and commitment so that Parliament and Canada can have a clearer idea of the direction the government is taking in international development.
We are now without an aid strategy. The 1975-1980 strategy paper has had no successor. It expired last year and there has been nothing to take its place. How are we supposed to determine what the long-term and comprehensive implication of the government's aid initiatives are if we cannot debate and scrutinize such issues, if they are not brought before the House as they should be through legislation?
Bill C-74, as the minister has explained and as I have mentioned, deals with financial commitments to certain international development banks and funds. As such it affects the division between multilateral and bilateral assistance. This is a very important aspect of our overall aid program: What weight will be given to multilateral programs and what weight will be given to bilateral programs? This determination should not be made in an ad hoc fashion. Rather, it should be part of a concrete, long-term program, one that is comprehensive, well thought out and will place our aid where it is most needed. In other words, where it will do the most good.
Such a comprehensive program was offered by the North-South task force report, the broad thrust of which the government has accepted. However, broad approval is not enough and I have brought that to the minister's attention in the House. What we need is a detailed strategy similar to the
1975-1980 strategy for international development. We could then at least measure the government's progress in this critical field.
Such a strategy should be based upon the recommendations of the North-South task force report and I think should rely on two fundamental beliefs. The first is the need for continuing and direct assistance to the very poorest countries in the world through Canadian developmental funds to countries which are becoming progressively poorer because of escalating oil costs and world-wide inflation. This should be the initial basis upon which we base our oil strategy.
The second basis on which to plan our development assistance to other nations is the need to enter into modern trading and financial relationships with the newly industrialized countries of the Third World so that they can consolidate the hard-won gains they have already achieved.
The bill before us today provides for certain borrowing by regional development banks of Canadian funds. I have said that my party approves of this measure, but I say to the minister how much more we would welcome the presentation by the government of a comprehensive developmental aid strategy for the decade of the 1980s.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT (FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS) ASSISTANCE ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has pointed out, Bill C-74 is in effect a companion piece to Bill C-71. Just as we supported Bill C-71 we shall also support Bill C-74.
I should like to refer again to a remark made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands by saying that we also agree that these developmental programs, in which Canada, we hope, will become more increasingly involved, ought to be within the confines of one department instead of fractionalized as they are at the present time. I realize that what happened is that some time ago the International Development Association Act was enacted. Therefore, any money that is sought under that legislation has to come by way of amendment to that act. But when it comes to international development assistance, since we do not already have an act of that description it is possible for the government to bring in a new one and to put it where it belongs, under the aegis of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan). Things that are under the aegis of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) have a tougher time than they do when they are under the responsibility of a minister interested in the subject itself.
I should also like to comment, as others have, on the reason we are dealing with these bills, which goes back to the ruling made by Madam Speaker regarding certain items in the estimates. If the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands will forgive me, I should like to make a slight correction in the way they described these matters. They both referred to them as dollar items which the Speaker ruled out. In some cases they
July 2, 1981

are dollar items, but in some cases they are items of quite substantial sums. In fact, one of the items before us right now is for $4 million. That is a lot more than a dollar. In other words, Madam Speaker in her ruling, in response to the points raised by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), said that it is not only improper to try to legislate by dollar items, but that it was also improper to try to arrange for the spending of large sums of money on conditions set out in an item in the estimates, which is, in effect, an attempt to use the estimates for the legislative process. I pay my respects to the hon. member for Calgary Centre for having raised these issues two or three times and having obtained the decision of Madam Speaker in this session.
I trust the concerned department will not make it necessary for us to go through this again in another session. I hope they will realize by amendments to existing acts or by the bringing in of new acts. We welcome the fact that we are doing it properly now, and just as the Official Opposition has said, we take the same position, that it is not our desire to drag out the discussion on these matters. We are glad to have the opportunity to deal with them in the right way. Mind you, it is easier for us to say that when it is something we really support.
That is the position in which we find ourselves with respect to both Bill C-71 and Bill C-74. We are strongly and wholly in favour of Canada enlarging her role in aid to the other parts of the world, but it is more than that, in playing our part in helping to bring about a better world right around the globe.
We have all been told thousands of times about the remark of Sir Wilfrid Laurier to the effect that the twentieth century would belong to Canada. I think the time has come for us to realize that the twenty-first century had better belong to humanity as a whole, or else there might not be a twenty-second century.
We can no longer go on with a world in which a quarter or a third of its people go to bed hungry every night. These are facts we have come to realize, and there has been some tremendous rhetoric about this right here in the House of Commons in this session. There was no better speech on the need for our being concerned in the North about the South, or in the better-off parts of the world for the other parts, than the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a few weeks ago. But the point we are trying to make from this side of the House this afternoon is that rhetoric is not enough.
We are happy to support the proposals in Bill C-71 and Bill C-74. We think that Canada's financial contribution, whether it is through developmental loans or outright aid and outright gifts, should be increased. But we think we must go a great deal further than that. In other words, we think we have to start planning our industrial strategy-another pair of words that gets thrown around a fair deal. We have to start planning our economy, not just with the thought of what it does for ourselves, for housing, health, education and so on in our country, but the part that it plays in bringing about improved living conditions around the world.
I have already indulged in quoting a few of the stock quotations there are around, but there is another one which
International Financial Assistance
comes to my mind, namely, that if you find a hungry man and you give him a fish, you provide a meal for him; but if you teach him how to fish, you provide meals down the road. Our industrial strategy, our economy, our trade, all our arrangements, at some point have to be made with the whole world in mind. We must start thinking in those terms.
Of course, we are quite interested in the Ottawa Summit Conference which will take place here in this city in a couple of weeks. We applaud the efforts of the Prime Minister to get some of the other heads of government who will be at that conference to show some real interest in North-South problems. We urge that he put everything he can into that effort. These conferences always end up with communiques of some sort. They sound good or make it appear as though they did something, but it really is something which has gone beyond the stage of speech-making or rhetoric. If we are to have a world that enjoys the twenty-first century, we must start thinking in terms of industrial strategy, trade, finance, economics and the rest of it, with a view to bringing about a really better world.
I notice it is five o'clock here in Ottawa and that means it is two o'clock in British Columbia. Out there this afternoon a funeral service is taking place about which Canadians right across this land are thinking. I was pleased when I noticed that the heading put on the tributes paid the other day to Terry Fox read "Tributes to a Magnificent Canadian". I suggest one of the reasons that Canadians are so anxious to pay the deepest respect and the deepest tribute they can to the memory of Terry Fox is that it tells us our young people really have got something. Terry Fox showed us that.
But I remind the House there are others. I think of the countless numbers of young Canadians who respond to the call of CUSO and who have gone out to other parts of the world to try to help bring about better conditions in Southeast Asia, Africa, South America and in various other countries. I think of other kinds of organizations under church auspices and under the auspices of non-governmental organizations, and so on. These attract our young people, who are sometimes described as belonging to the "me" generation. They have got pretty good stuff in them.
I think we should recognize that there is no longer any need to say that charity has to begin at home or to ask why do we tax people to help those abroad? I believe the young people today who will be taking charge of things in Canada not many years hence want to play their part in building that better world. In my younger days that was expressed by joining the various missionary movements and in going to different parts of the world. For a time it was to go as propagandists for a particular faith. That soon grew into the provision of teachers and agricultural experts, engineers and doctors, most of whom two or three generations ago went out to other parts of the world under religious auspices; but the feeling we are our brother's keeper was there in those days and it is there now.

July 2, 1981

I am satisfied that just as we are honouring the memory of a magnificent Canadian out in Port Coquitlam this afternoon so too can we count on our young people today wanting us to play our part in changing the whole world from a place where millions go to bed hungry every night to a place where there are opportunities for development and a decent life in terms of jobs, education, health and security. We can do it. That is what we are talking about this afternoon.
That is why we are prepared to support these two bills. But we call upon the government in the not too distant future to come back before us with something much more expansive and imaginative. For indeed, just as the twentieth century did provide a lot for us in Canada, so the twenty-first must bring about a better world for all our people, and we Canadians want to play a real and effective part in that role.

Yes, I am deeply interested.
The Maritime Freight Rates Act, referred to from now on as the MFRA, and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, to which I will refer as the ARFAA, together provide for a program of transportation subsidies in the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe peninsula. Total expenditures under this program amounted to about $62.6 million in 1980-81. The MFRA has been in existence since 1927 and applies only to rail traffic. The ARFAA was passed in 1969 and extends the subsidy program to truckers.
To complicate matters a little bit, the ARFAA also contains features which link the two acts and are designed to control those features and the level of subsidy expenditures. For one, the rail subsidy on certain commodities can be reduced or eliminated. As a matter of fact, it has been reduced, for example, from 20 per cent to 15 per cent. There can be a reduction of the rate of subsidy. That is one feature. Another one is that the amount of subsidy paid annually to truckers cannot exceed the amount saved by reducing or eliminating the rail subsidy. The ceiling is established under section 6(2) of the act. That ceiling is the subject for today.
However, after the ARFAA came into effect, I repeat in 1969, the rail subsidy was not reduced as much as planned. Things did not turn out exactly as they were meant to turn out. The number of truckers eligible for subsidy under the ARFAA grew dramatically. Just to give Your Honour an illustration, in 1969 there were 450 truckers in the area. In 1980, we had 3,800. Obviously, because of the highway strengthening programs and other factors, the number of shippers using trucks in the area multiplied extraordinarily. The result was that, if the ceiling were applied, truckers would get proportionately less than the railways, creating an inequity between two modes, which the ARFAA was designed, in principle, to redress.
I might add that somewhere in the meantime, in 1967, we had the National Transportation Act, which specifically says that there should not be discrimination between different modes of transportation.
In some ways, that ceiling on trucking subsidies, related to the subsidy reduction on railways, was discrimination against
July 2, 1981

the truckers in favour of the railways. I am saying all that to try somehow to justify why the practice to ignore the ceiling was established. It therefore became the practice from 197172 to include an item in the estimates which, in fact, removed that ceiling. It is included in the old estimates in the following words:
-and to provide that subsection 6(2) of the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act shall not apply in the case of the payment of assistance in the current fiscal year to truckers pursuant to subsection 6(1) of that Act.
These were the words tagged at the end of that estimate which had the effect of removing the ceiling for practical purposes.
It is estimated that in 1981-82 the savings from the reduction in the rail subsidy will be about $14 million. This is the saving which establishes a relationship between the truckers and the railways. I repeat that it will be about $14 million. The amount which would be paid to truckers without the ceiling is about $43 million. So there is a potential $29 million shortfall in the amount of subsidies paid if the ceiling is enforced. In other words, it costs $29 million not to enforce the ceiling.
As I have already indicated, it was the practice to remove the statutory ceiling through the estimates, and that practice was ruled out by the Speaker recently. Bill C-73, which is in front of us now, has the effect of removing the ceiling by proper statutory means so that the trucking subsidy can continue to be paid in full. Recipients who have invested on the basis of a continued subsidy could reasonably argue that its abrupt termination without advance notice of a change in policy would be unduly harsh.
This bill notwithstanding, the program as a whole is under review. I am quite sure the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) also looked at it. Some people wonder if there would not be savings to be made there without damaging the economy of the region covered by these two acts. Officials are now carefully studying the possibility of further selective reductions in order to reduce expenditures without detracting, as I said, from the purpose of the program, which is to assist the transportation of goods in the Atlantic provinces and the Gaspe peninsula. At present, the program as a whole is believed to be beneficial to the area, and any substantial change would, of course, be preceded by full consultation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE TO TRUCKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset, I would like to thank the hon. minister for giving us an explanation of the details of this bill I suppose that that is certainly one positive element to this process, getting an explanation and some historic background to the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act and the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
We on this side have no fundamental objection to this piece of legislation. However, what we do object to is the procedure which has become the practice of this government in terms of dealing with a matter which should be properly dealt with in legislation in the first place.
Atlantic Region Freight Assistance
As the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) indicated, the purpose of this bill and the purpose of vote 110 was to remove the ceiling which would allow the truckers to get sufficient subsidy to provide equality in treatment to the two competing modes of transportation. I know that there are people in this House who would object to a provision which would provide for unfair treatment between two respective modes of transport; and they are competing modes.
However, it brings me to the over-all thrust of the debate on these pieces of legislation, the series of bills with which we are dealing as a result of the work and the scrutiny of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). It is really a classic demonstration of how this government continues, in a very blatant way, to erode the rights, the privileges and the powers of Parliament. This is not the first time that this government has been caught using methods which are less than legitimate. It has really become almost a chronic rule-breaker when it comes to avoiding and circumventing the parliamentary process.
I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will allude to this in more detail than I; but the rights and privileges of members of Parliament have been eroded. Indeed, the institution of Parliament has been undermined over the years in its ability to control public expenditures. By the way in which we handle our estimates, it seems to have become nothing more than a rubber stamp. At this time it is necessary to build confidence and trust in our Canadian institutions, particularly our political and parliamentary institutions. It certainly bothers me to see a government move continuously and incessantly along the road toward that undermining process. I think that it is fundamentally repugnant to the principle of parliamentary democracy. Once again, I think that we, as members of this House, and certainly as members of the Canadian electorate who support the continued strength of the parliamentary process, owe a great deal of debt and gratitude to the hon. member for Calgary Centre.
Not too long ago a former auditor general stated in one of his annual reports that Parliament had lost or was close to losing control of the public purse. In view of these backhanded strategies, it is little wonder that he made that remark. Indeed, it is little wonder that Canadians, by and large, are suspicious of the way we deal with taxpayers' money. We are really trustees of their money. We are the guardians of the public purse.
I welcome this piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, and I welcome the fact that equality of treatment is maintained. We are not opposed to the expenditure but, I repeat, we are fundamentally opposed to the process. It is the duty of Parliament to pass laws; Parliament is responsible for the authorization of expenditure and for the collection of moneys.
We see in Madam Speaker's ruling that vote 110 sought an amendment to existing legislation, which was clearly out of order. We have other examples of that when we look at what is going on with respect to the establishment of VIA Rail. That is

July 2, 1981
Atlantic Region Freight Assistance
a question that must come up for debate in due course in this House.
1 am very interested in the exchange that has been going on between the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the co-chairmen of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
I hope that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is listening because, as he pointed out quite correctly, what we are dealing with here are not dollar items but items that were included in the Main Estimates. VIA Rail, which has become the instrument for the operation and maintenance and supply of rail passenger service in this country, was established through the process of a one-dollar vote in the House of Commons. In the Votes and Proceedings for June 15, 1981 this is dealt with at page 2464.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that I am deviating somewhat from the thrust of the bill but we are dealing with the fundamental parliamentary principle that this House should consider legislation, expenditures and the collection of revenue in a proper and just manner.
The committee had four objections to the way in which VIA Rail was established. The committee reported, at page 2464, of Votes and Proceedings, as follows:
VIA Rail Canada Inc. has been established and set up in business-and in consequence almost all the railway passenger services of the country have been brought into government ownership, control and funding-pursuant to an involved use of subordinate powers, a dollar vote in an Appropriation Act and the three slim regulations under report. At no time has Parliament had the opportunity to debate and to settle what are very significant matters.
I am directing this criticism to the government, Mr. Speaker, and not to the Minister of Transport because he was not a member of cabinet at that time. Knowing the integrity and honour of the minister, I am sure that if he had been minister at that time he would not have circumvented the parliamentary process. At page 2465 of Votes and Proceedings there appears the following:
The whole authority for public funding of the VIA Rail operation and its takeover of railway passenger services provided by railway companies rests in the dollar vote, vote 52d, Department of Transport, Appropriation Act No. 1, 1977, which reads as follows:
Then it basically describes the manner in which the company is to be set up under the provision of a one dollar vote. Then there appears the following passage:
Upon this foundation hangs now all the law and the administration of almost all railway passenger services in Canada.
What a devious way to create a Crown corporation which is all-encompassing! The committee report goes on at page 2467 as follows:
In your committee's judgment, the settling of the legal regime to govern the now publicly owned, controlled and funded railway passenger service is too important a matter to be left to the corporate policy, and virtually unlimited corporate powers, of VIA Rail Canada Inc., a corporation wholly owned by the Crown, and to skeletal regulations made under a dollar vote which in the nature of procedure in the House of Commons cannot have been subjected to significant debate. Parliament should have been, and still should be, given the opportunity to debate the future and structure of railway passenger services in Canada and the manner of their management and control; and your committee is inclined to believe that this should include the maintenance of the jurisdiction of the
Canadian Transport Commission over VIA Rail Canada. As things stand now, even if a bill to regulate railway passenger services and VIA Rail Canada Inc. were to be introduced, many important matters have been effectively foreclosed from Parliament's debate and disposition by the extensive and pre-emptive executive action that has already been taken. It is objectionable in principle that relationships between the new public railway passenger authority and the railway commpanies, and the take-over of services, should have been settled without parliamentary involvement.
Those are very profound words, Mr. Speaker. It is interesting to note that the minister, who is now attempting to reduce the level of subsidy, is really choosing the course to which this committee takes very serious objection. The government is now attempting to circumvent the regulatory party, the CTC, by deciding, through cabinet deliberations, which lines will provide service and which will be abandoned. That is fundamentally repugnant to the principle of parliamentary democracy.
The committee then quoted from the proceedings of an earlier committee, reported at page 2467 as follows:
"In the review of statutory instruments the Committee has been struck by the number of instances of the use of Votes in Appropriation Acts as vehicles for the conferring of subordinate law-making powers, usually upon the governor in council. From 1st January 1972 to 30th June 1976 at least one hundred and four items of delegated legislation have to the knowledge of the Committee, been made pursuant to Votes. (The task of adding up the number is not easy since spent regulations are removed from the Index to Part II of The Canada Gazette at the end of each calendar year in which their effect became spent.) The committee fears that many, many more examples exist which have not been classed by the Crown's legal advisers as statutory instruments and of the existence of which the committee has neither knowledge nor the means of knowledge."
There follows a very damning indictment of the process that has been used by this government to circumvent parliamentary control.
Now I come to the Minister of Transport, Mr. Speaker. There has been a continuing exchange of correspondence between the co-chairmen of the committee and the minister, beginning in June, 1980. The co-chairmen asked the minister to bring in a bill to provide for the incorporation of VIA Rail. In August, 1980 the minister responded that he anticipated a cabinet decision on the issue would be available by the end of September, 1980. In November, 1980 a letter was addressed to the minister asking what progress had been made. I quote in part from the letter, which appears at page 2470 as follows:
We were instructed to ask whether the Cabinet decision to which you referred has been taken and when you will respond to the committee's position on the need for the introduction of a VIA Rail Canada bill.
On January 12, 1981, the minister replied in part, as follows:
I expect the matter to be discussed early in the new year. Once a decision has been reached, I will advise your Committee on the requirement for a VIA Rail Canada bill.
It was dated January 12, 1981. Then we have further correspondence. The final letter reported here indicates that a decision is not available and furthermore it is considered that the VIA Rail act is not needed.

At a time when our parliamentary institutions are under attack, it is incumbent upon the government to ensure that it proceeds in a proper parliamentary fashion.
With regard to the matter of expenditure of funds, whether it is for legitimate and good purpose or provokes some questions in debate, it is important that the adjudication of those issues be left to members of Parliament. The power should be transferred back to the elected representatives, the members of Parliament, so that they can properly debate the issues.
The debate this afternoon has provided information. It gives members an opportunity to review and assess the effectiveness of a given program. If we have done nothing further, we have had the opportunity to assess and analyse one program that has been in effect since 1927 and another since 1969. Had the minister realized he was going to have to bring in legislation to deal with that issue, he may have seen fit to broaden the legislation so that we could have had a debate on the pros and cons and determined ways and means by which the program may be instituted more effectively, in other words transforming the impact of that program to meet the needs and challenges of the 1980s rather than the 1920s.
I appreciate your tolerance, Mr. Speaker. I realize I have transcended the rules of relevance to some extent. Nevertheless, I feel very strongly about this issue. If nothing else, I hope that the series of debates that have been created as a result of the deliberations on these very important bills will give us the opportunity to
Atlantic Region Freight Assistance
look at some reform in the legislative process and the whole process of dealing with legislation. We could do it in such a way that the programs that are in effect can be applied to modern day realities and perhaps be more relevant and effective. In the process, the role and the power of the elected representatives will be strengthened.

speechtext:
that Bill C-72, to amend the National Housing Act, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there are two clauses to the bill. They are very brief and touch upon two operations of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and also implement two very important programs of the National Housing Act. I might say, they are well received in Canada from coast to coast.
The two sections of the National Housing Act involved are Section 34.14(2) which concerns the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, referred to as RRAP, and Section 40(5) which has to do with the production of low rental housing and the acquisition and development of land for housing purposes under federal-provincial agreements. Those are in essence the two clauses: clause 1 dealing with the RRAP program and clause 2 dealing with assisted rental.
Dealing with the first clause, the legislation now provides that the total amount of loans made by the corporation for the purposes of RRAP may not exceed SI00 million unless authorized by Parliament. As rehabilitation costs and loan limits have increased over the years, and greater numbers of people have participated, the corporation has had to increase its borrowing in order to continue to finance the program on the government's behalf.
The borrowing limit has been increased over the years by a vote under this estimates. Increases authorized in this way have raised the limit from $100 million to $170 million. Vote L70 in the 1981-82 estimates would have increased the limit by another $59.8 million to a total of $230.5 million, which is the figure in clause 1 of Bill C-72 before us.
In generally describing the program and the increase, I should like to say that scarcely does a day go by that I do not have a request from a member of this House, whether from the government side or from parties opposite. The program is popular and obviously serves a need in the community, as witnessed by the demand. It addresses an aspect of housing which, I think, will take on more significance in the future, that is the repair, maintenance and upkeep of existing stock rather than the direction of new starts in housing which we have witnessed at quite a remarkable strength through the last 20 or 30 years.
The situation regarding Section 40(5), and that relates to the second clause, is similar. The National Housing Act imposes a limit of $150 million on advances obtained by the corporation for meeting its share of the capital cost of federal-provincial housing projects. Over the years, by means of a vote under estimates, this limit has been increased from $150 million to almost $1.4 billion. I think that figure illustrates the need met by such a program under agreements, in co-operation and in conjunction with provincial governments.
I think I should suggest to those people who complain that this government does not have a commitment to assist Canadians with housing that they should well consider that this program is one of the most worth-while programs, although, needless to say, it is very expensive at the rate of $1.4 billion. Although the public housing program is no longer active in all provinces, the section of the act is applied to supporting rural and native housing programs and servicing of lands held by the federal-provincial partnership prior to their sale. Mainly for these reasons the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation sought in the 1981-82 estimates to increase the limits on its borrowings by a further $112.5 million to a total of just over $1.5 billion. Clause 2(a) of Bill C-72 before us specifies the amount of $1,504,500,000.
In conclusion I would like to say, as I began, that these are two very important programs of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They illustrate and demonstrate the commitment of the government to continued responsibility in housing, and I know that the programs are supported by all members in this House. Otherwise we would not be asking for the increases I have referred to. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and address a few remarks to the bill. I will endeavour to make my remarks relevant. However, I want to explain to the House why we are supporting the bill.
The bill is divided into two main parts. The first deals with the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and the second with public housing.
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the minister. He made reference to requests from all sides of the House for assistance to the public with respect to housing. I appreciate that the requests from his side of the House must be as numerous and worthwhile as those from this side, and I appreciate that the government is paying lip service, in any event, by raising ceilings to a commitment to public housing. However, I would like to say to the minister that the raising of a ceiling does not indicate commitment. What matters is what is done, within the limits this House approves-with the programs the government will bring forward in addition to the current very worth-while programs, to substantiate the spending of money. It is not exactly raising the ceiling but what is supporting the ceiling that hon. members on this side of the House are interested in.
I and others in this House have been very critical of the government with respect to the chaos in the housing sector today. In terms of housing starts, which are technically up but literally down, in April the pre-sales contractors across Canada had translated the housing starts into a boom-on paper-but we know they will flatten out in the latter months of the summer because builders are just not building "spec" houses any more. As a result, emphasis on residential rehabilitation is very important, and for that reason our party is pleased to support this bill.
We also have problems, which the Liberal interest rate policy is causing throughout the country, with respect to mortgage interest rates. The rate is now at a record Liberal high of 18.5 per cent. People are just not buying new homes any more. They are forced to stay where they are, and the maintenance of rental housing is becoming all important to Canada. I point out that we are talking about rehabilitating housing and about vacancy rates; this government has created a real crisis with respect to apartment vacancy rates.
In April, 1979 the vacancy rate in Canada was 3.6 per cent. The acceptable average across Canada is 3 per cent. In April, 1981, by dint of indifference and by a real and determined effort at nothing at all, this government has brought the vacancy rate down to 1.8 per cent. In areas such as metro Toronto, which the minister represents, it is 0.4 per cent. People across Canada are having a difficult time finding places to live. It is no longer a question of adequate and decent shelter; it is a question of finding a place to live. For that reason we are certainly prepared to support this program.
We know that older housing requires extensive renovation. We have reviewed the very excellent report prepared for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation entitled "An evaluation of RRAP," which is the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. I have looked with interest at some of the recommendations in the report. I note, for example, that the eligibility under RRAP has changed. It is interesting to me as
National Housing Act
the spokesman for housing on this side of the House that the number one recommendation on page 121 has been adopted by the government, and I commend the government for that. It is also interesting to note that the income limit for family homes has been increased from $6,000 to $9,000. It is very unfortunate that AHOP owners who were led down the garden path in 1976 have found that this very same government-there has been a 50 per cent increase-has decided, instead of using 25 per cent of family income as the upper limit for AHOP eligibility, to raise that limit to 30 per cent. On behalf of the thousands of Canadian home owners who are renewing their mortgages under AHOP I suggest to the government that it would do very well to go back to the standard of 25 per cent on the basis of which these people were inveigled into buying homes and to go back to its original principles and take a hard look at the funding which is provided within this ceiling.
The minister referred to co-operation between federal and provincial levels. We do not want to see the same thing happen to this program that happened to the community services contribution program, under which muncipalities across Canada entered into three-phase programs with the understanding that the Government of Canada would stand behind its commitment to the cities, towns and villages of Canada to provide services. The government pulled out of the program and left municipalities across Canada high and dry looking for funding for two and three-phase programs in which they had become involved at the exhortation of the government. Many municipalities involved in this program have gone to a considerable amount of effort to set up their procedures, and I suggest that the government consider seriously the termination of these programs, if they are terminated, on a very orderly basis.
As far as the public housing part of the bill is concerned, we are supportive of anything this government does to help Canadians find decent, affordable housing in sound community environments. We on this side know that the shelter allowance has been the favourite trial balloon of this government. Shelter allowances have been created and hiked prior to national housing conferences only to have the balloon deflated two weeks later when the conferences were over and all the delegates had gone home. I hope this government under this increased ceiling will take a hard look at shelter allowances, their impact on the municipalities of Canada, just what sort of public funding they have put into place and what sort of co-operation will be required on the part of provincial governments.
We think there is a lot of merit in a shelter allowance program. We want to see the details which will be brought forward, and I hope when we are approving an increase in funding from $150 million to $1,504,500,000 this money will be spent wisely. I can assure the government we will be very interested not only in the ceiling but also in the supports holding up the ceiling in the future. I thank the House for allowing me to address it on this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak briefly about this matter and to address its two main

July 2, 1981
National Housing Act
elements. One thing which always concerns me about rehabilitation programs is the way they are apportioned. In the main, given current economic conditions, I think the future will be even more difficult for people.
Let me go back a minute. Generally speaking, rehabilitation programs are undertaken after the sale of a house. Someone purchases a house and decides to modernize it or do some work in it before moving into it. Unless there is a dramatic downturn in interest rates and a new and more innovative way of providing mortgage funds, and unless people are able to assume mortgages at or about 25 per cent of their income, I suspect we will find that a large number of people moving into homes which could qualify under this rehabilitation program will not be able to afford them. I suspect what will happen then is that this will become another program for those ever so slightly more affluent than the average, although I hope that is not so. For those people in the city core because it is the only place they can live, for those in older homes because it is the best they can afford, given the current economic conditions in housing even a program such as this does not provide them with an opportunity for access.
As I said in another debate, I think at some point it might be useful to do a further evaluation of the socio-economic group which is able to take advantage of this rehabilitation program funding to determine whether people on a limited income but who want to own a home of their own can gain access to a program such as this for the purpose of upgrading, improving and thereby stabilizing some of the core areas of our larger cities. I am sure my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) can think of such areas in his own riding, as I can in mine, where rehabilitation programs would be very worthwhile. We would want to encourage people to undertake the kind of rehabilitation that will keep the houses in a good state of repair so that they are an asset to the owner and the community. The unfortunate part, as I am sure my colleague will agree with me, is that for a large number of people living in those areas the thought of assuming yet another financial burden is impossible. They just cannot do it.
So while we support the program and understand that additional funding is a necessity given the changing times, I say to the minister we think a serious look should be taken at who is able to take advantage of it and at the ways it can be better utilized, and then perhaps we should consider setting down some additional guidelines for that portion of this expenditure and for public housing in general.
I want to talk about that for a moment because I think it is a vital area of concern. Given the economic conditions I have just spoken about, I suspect that unless we see some very dramatic changes in house prices and mortgage interest rates, there will be an overwhelming growth in the need for public housing. Large numbers of people who have never considered public housing will be put in a position of having to make that choice. I do not think that is necessarily a bad choice, but they will have to do it despite their own preference. I say to the
minister that this $1.5 billion, though it is a substantial sum, will pale into insignificance over the course of the next decade when measured against the dollars needed to provide the public housing units required to meet the rapidly increasing demand which will result from the other more general government policies directly affecting housing.
I think housing, like health, education and food, has to be given priority by the government. It cannot be dealt with in a frivolous or thoughtless way. It cannot just be allowed to happen by some mystic means. We cannot leave it up to the private sector to grapple with the ever-increasing costs of providing housing. We know full well we are not keeping pace with what the demand is undoubtedly going to be. I think every member of this House believes, Mr. Speaker, that owning a home is part of the Canadian heritage, if you will. Those people who were able to move from public housing into their own home will not be able to do that in the future. Therefore, there is no doubt in my mind that the future will require that we look seriously at new and innovative ways of developing a housing bank, if you will, which will provide an opportunity for people to buy a home at a price they can afford and in an area where they would like to live.
I can see the changes taking place now, as I am sure every member of this House can, changes in the metropolitan areas owing to the fact there is a money crunch and there are fewer and fewer rental accommodations being built and fewer and fewer people able to enter the housing market because of the problem of trying to meet their commitments in the face of the tremendous costs being levied against home ownership.
I hope we will have from the minister in the near future some exciting new and innovative housing policies. I say to him that MURBs do not really count in this. That program does not even begin to address the problems because the people I speak about will just not be able to move into even that kind of housing. While this change appears to be very significant on the surface, when you look at it in comparison to the expenditures of last year and the year before, it is not as dramatic a change as you might think. I suspect it will do little more than enable the housing corporation to keep pace with inflation and do something marginal in terms of meeting the ever-increasing demand.
We must rethink our entire policy as it relates to housing for people. What we have before us met the needs of another era. It met the needs of an era when 25 per cent of an individual's income was enough to purchase a home. Nowadays 25 per cent of a single income would hardly get one into an apartment, let alone allow one to buy a home. Since we are part of the problem, we have an obligation to make an effort to become part of the solution.
The over-all economic conditions may well ameliorate over time. Perhaps things will improve, but I suspect the improvement will be gradual and that it will not enable a large number of people to attain for themselves what we would all like to see for every Canadian family, that is, not that they necessarily
July 2, 1981

purchase homes for themselves but at least that they have the opportunity to do so.
This program will be under serious pressure. The minister should devote a great deal of his time between now and next fall to preparing for the onslaught. I am certain there will be a major debate in the House next fall. At least there will be a debate among the public of Canada who cannot find places to stay at prices they can afford. There will be major debate on why the government has allowed housing to become a luxury rather than a necessity.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INCREASE IN ADVANCE PAYMENTS LIMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you and hon. members opposite who have spoken on this housing bill. In particular I thank them for their support for the increase identified under the two programs respecting residential rehabilitation and public housing. I believe both speakers who preceded me identified the demand and the need. There has been recognition that the cumulative costs from year to year represent a significant undertaking by the government.
Generally I should like to speak to an issue which was raised by both speakers, that is, the role of the provinces. Recently in Ottawa I had an opportunity to meet with my counterparts, the provincial ministers responsible for housing. I drew to their attention the fact that the government had made some moves by increasing budgets and taking new steps in response to difficult times. I asked where was the provincial response, for example, to the MURB or to the government moving toward increasing its commitment under AHOP and ARP. Admittedly it is not sufficient by the calculation of some hon. members, but nonetheless it is an increase by the government. I made an observation concerning the provincial response to the difficult time we are experiencing in housing. If all provinces responded in the same way to the situation, if the unevenness in the provincial response were eliminated, they would be addressing regional pressures brought about by the movement of people from one province to another.
As I have indicated, rehabilitation offers a very important potential for the future housing industry. It is for that reason that CMHC reports monthly on statistics showing starts and activities in new housing. They will be reporting this month for the first time, and quarterly thereafter, on the experience across the country regarding residential rehabilitation.
Business of the House
I should like to offer some comfort to the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). Although he is fearful that people at all income levels are not taking advantage of the residential rehabilitation potential, if he compared the first quarter of this year with the first quarter of last year he would find that there has been threefold increase in activity nationally. In conclusion, I know there has been criticism about the MURB provision reintroduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in his budget, that it did not encompass people with modest incomes. It was not designed to cover that group. For example, the move to increase the number of housing starts under section 56(1) was a tailor-made response of the government to that area. I thank the House for its indulgence.
